text:
The global obesity epidemic has relentlessly 
pushed the incidence of lipid-​related disor-
ders to new heights. Data from a 2018 report 
suggest that nearly 25% of adults globally have 
non-​alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)1. 
Moreover, an estimated 17 million people 
worldwide die each year from cardio­vascular 
disease2. Although lipid-​lowering and 
weight-​loss strategies have shown efficacy 
in combating these diseases, they have been 
inconsis­tently successful, which is probably 
owing to the complex nature of lipid homeo­
stasis. The present study3 applied an omics-​
driven strategy to identify new players in the 
control of hepatic steatosis.
Disease pathophysiology is the result of 
genetic and environmental interactions, and 
mouse genetic reference panels have become 
the tool of choice to interrogate the influence 
of genetic variation on disease traits, while 
maintaining a constant common environ-
ment. Researchers use panels of hundreds 
of mouse strains to identify genetic modi­
fiers of complex disease phenotypes4–7. Major 
advances in omics-​scale approaches have 
facilitated ‘big data’ integration, with the goal 
of understanding disease pathophysiology 
and/or identifying biomarkers for diagnosis 
or monitoring disease status.
The new study by Parker and colleagues3 
sought to identify genetic modifiers of hepatic 
lipid accumulation (steatosis) using multi-​
omics analyses of 107 inbred mouse strains. 
The authors integrated liver and plasma 
lipidomic profiles with liver proteome and 
genetic polymorphism data. Validating their 
approach, the authors’ analysis identified 
protein) as a regulator of hepatic steatosis 
through cross-​referencing single nucleo-
tide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with 
lipid (lipid quantitative trait loci (QTLs)) and 
protein (protein QTLs) levels. Interestingly, 
genetic variation in PSMD9 was previously 
associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus 
risk in humans8. Functional genomic analy-
sis in two mouse strains demonstrated that 
PSMD9 controls hepatic and plasma lipid 
metabolism in a strain-​specific manner, 
in part by regulating hepatic lipogenesis. 
These findings illustrate the utility of such 
big-​data-driven approaches.
Despite the wealth of data in the present 
study, several avenues for further investiga-
tion and data mining of this resource remain. 
Although also a point of originality, the use of 
proteome data is a clear limitation of the pres-
ent study. Among the 7,775 proteins identi-
fied, only 4,311 were quantified in more than 
50 mouse strains, thereby representing a clear 
bias towards proteins with favourable mass-​
spectrometry-identification characteristics. 
Moreover, the mice used in this study were 
sacrificed and analysed following an overnight 
fast. Contrary to humans, overnight fasting 
in mice leads to a catabolic state, which can 
result in >10% body weight loss. Consequently, 
overnight fasting drives a physiological steato-
sis that originates from free fatty acid release 
by adipose tissue. Thus, the observed varia-
tions in hepatic lipid content between mouse 
strains might also be linked to alterations in 
adipose tissue function, an unexplored aspect 
in the present study. In addition, it is also 
unclear whether alterations in the so-​called 
‘toxic’ lipids (ceramides, triacylglycerols and 
diacylglycerols) are actually linked to disease 
susceptibility in the different studied mouse 
strains. Indeed, the complex link between 
alterations in hepatic lipid metabolism and the 
progression of steatosis to pathological non- 
​alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) remains an 
area of intense research.
In terms of data analysis, the presented 
approach explored associations between 
hepatic lipid species, protein abundance and 
SNPs, which is clearly a unique, unbiased 
approach capable of identifying relevant play-
ers in lipid metabolism. Another interesting 
strategy would be a targeted approach to iden-
tify proteins that might control specific lipid 
species in a given pathway. Gene–metabolite 
data integration is now routinely performed 
several subcellular and functional pathways 
that are implicated in lipid metabolism. 
Correlation of the protein abundance of 
known and unknown proteins allowed the 
prediction of the subcellular localization of 
proteins whose localization was previously 
unknown. Moreover, a machine-​learning 
approach was used to identify plasma lipid 
signatures that are linked to steatosis, thereby 
yielding potential biomarkers of hepatic lipid 
metabolism. Among the analysed lipid classes, 
triacylglycerol species correlated best between 
plasma and liver, an expected finding given 
the major contribution of liver-​derived VLDL 
production to plasma triacylglycerol content 
under fasting conditions.
This study is one of the largest to date in 
terms of number of mouse strains and lipids 
(>300 species) profiled. The main strength 
of the study lies in the fact that, unlike pre-
vious works6,7, the authors used proteome, 
instead of transcriptome data. As many 
enzymes involved in lipid metabolism are 
also regulated at the post-​transcriptional 
level, this approach might provide more 
physiologically relevant information. This 
hypothesis is confirmed by the identifica-
tion of PSMD9 (a proteasome-​associated

Understanding lipid metabolism 
through hepatic steat-​omics
Joel T. Haas    and Bart Staels   
Alterations in lipid metabolism are closely linked to disorders such as 
cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus and non-​alcoholic fatty liver 
disease. A multi-​omics study on a mouse genetic reference panel uncovers 
regulatory networks and potential biomarkers of hepatic lipid metabolism.
Refers to Parker, B. L. et al. An integrative systems genetic analysis of mammalian lipid metabolism. Nature 567, 187–193 
(2019).

in the analysis of classic biochemical path-
ways, such as glycolysis and the tricarboxylic 
acid cycle, owing to the relative simplicity of 
the enzyme–substrate relationship (that is, 
one substrate, one enzyme and one product) 
in these pathways. By contrast, the 42 tria-
cylglycerol species studied here are synthe-
sized by only two enzymes (diacylglycerol 
O-​acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1) and DGAT2) 
that use an even larger range of diacylglyc-
erol and acyl-​CoA substrates. More work is 
clearly needed to link lipid species differences 
to changes in the biochemical pathways that 
drive their metabolism.
Finally, the translational relevance of the 
findings of Parker and colleagues is only min-
imally explored. The authors found modest 
correlations between plasma and hepatic 
triacylglycerol and diacylglycerol content in 
both mice and in humans, though prediction 
of other hepatic lipid species (for example, 
ceramides) was much less reliable. The addi-
tional value of plasma lipidomic measures 
for diagnosis of hepatic steatosis, especially 
in light of widely available ultrasound and 
can only be assessed by invasive biopsy (that 
is, hepatocellular ballooning and fibrosis)9,10. 
The current study does not provide insight 
in the role of the identified pathways in the 
progression from hepatic steatosis to this 
active disease state, nor their utility as poten-
tial biomarkers for NASH, especially given 
that known players in NAFLD (that is, 
PNPLA3, MBOAT7 and TM6SF2) were not 
identified by the authors’ analysis.
Despite these limitations, the present study 
provides a comprehensive catalogue of lipid, 
protein and genetic data, constituting a valu-
able resource for future studies of hepatic lipid 
metabolism.
